text: ISTANBUL (Reuters) - A total of 136 individuals were taken into custody by Turkey on Thursday, with many being former military personnel, police officers, and educators, as part of four distinct operations targeting suspected affiliations with last year’s coup attempt, according to the state-run Anadolu news agency. The primary operation, which focused on the capital city of Ankara, resulted in the apprehension of 60 ex-security officials and extended across 30 provinces, Anadolu reported. Additionally, another operation that commenced on Wednesday in Diyarbakir led to the detention of 55 soldiers and affected 26 other provinces. Authorities are still pursuing one more suspect. In the northern regions of Samsun and Karabuk, six individuals were detained, alongside 15 educators in Ankara, as indicated by Anadolu. The individuals in question are alleged to have utilized the encrypted messaging application, ByLock, which the government claims was associated with the network of Fethullah Gulen, a cleric residing in the United States. The Turkish government holds Gulen responsible for orchestrating the failed coup attempt in July 2016, a claim he has denied while condemning the coup. In the wake of the July 2016 coup, over 50,000 individuals, including military, police, and civil service members, have been imprisoned awaiting trial, and approximately 150,000 others have faced dismissal or suspension. This extensive crackdown has raised concerns among Turkey's Western partners and human rights organizations, who argue that President Tayyip Erdogan is leveraging the coup as a means to suppress opposition. The government maintains that these actions, which were enacted under emergency conditions following the coup, are essential due to the security challenges facing Turkey.
source_text: Turkey detains 136 for suspected ties to coup plotters: agency. ISTANBUL (Reuters) - Turkey detained 136 people, including former police, teachers and soldiers, in four separate operations on Thursday over suspected links to last year s attempted military coup, the state-run Anadolu news agency said. Authorities detained 60 former security officials in the operation centered in the capital Ankara and spread over 30 provinces, Anadolu said. In a separate operation that began on Wednesday and centered on Diyarbakir and spread over 26 other provinces, 55 soldiers were detained, Anadolu said. Officials were still searching for one more suspect. Six others were detained in the northern provinces of Samsun and Karabuk, as well as 15 teachers in Ankara, Anadolu said. The suspects were alleged to be using the encrypted messaging app, ByLock, which the government says was used by the network of U.S.-based cleric Fethullah Gulen. Ankara blames Gulen, for orchestrating the failed coup in July 2016. Gulen has denied involvement and denounced the putsch. More than 50,000 people, including police, military personnel and civil servants, have been jailed pending trial in the aftermath of the July 2016 coup. Some 150,000 people were sacked or suspended. The crackdown has alarmed Turkey s Western allies and rights groups, who say President Tayyip Erdogan is using the coup as a pretext to muzzle dissent. The government says the measures, taken under emergency rule that was imposed after the coup, are necessary due to the security threats Turkey faces.

text: A historic agreement was reached on Wednesday, under which the United States will provide $38 billion in military aid to Israel over the next ten years, marking the largest military assistance package in U.S. history. According to a senior U.S. official, this deal will enable Israel, Washington’s primary ally in the Middle East, to enhance much of its fighter aircraft, boost the mobility of its ground forces, and fortify its missile defense systems. The package is the most substantial military aid ever granted by the U.S. to any nation, but it requires certain concessions from Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, as confirmed by officials from both nations. These concessions include Israel's commitment to refrain from requesting additional funding from Congress beyond the sum guaranteed in this new agreement and the gradual termination of a special arrangement that permitted Israel to allocate part of its U.S. aid to its domestic defense sector rather than exclusively on American arms. The negotiations, which spanned nearly ten months, highlighted ongoing tensions between President Barack Obama and Netanyahu, particularly regarding last year's U.S.-brokered nuclear agreement with Iran, which Netanyahu opposed. Additionally, the two nations have experienced disagreements over Palestinian issues. However, Netanyahu opted to establish a new agreement with Obama, who will leave office in January, rather than risk less favorable terms with the incoming U.S. administration, whether it is Democrat Hillary Clinton or Republican Donald Trump. This new deal allows him to circumvent uncertainties surrounding the future president and provides Israel’s defense sector with the opportunity to strategize for the long term. Obama’s advisors aimed to finalize a new deal before the conclusion of his presidency, viewing it as a significant element of his legacy. Critics from the Republican party contend that he has not been sufficiently attentive to Israel’s security needs, a claim the White House firmly disputes, asserting that he has been overly stringent with Netanyahu. The memorandum of understanding, which covers U.S. fiscal years 2019-2028, replaces the existing $30 billion MOU established in 2007, which concludes at the end of fiscal 2018. In a written statement, Obama remarked, “Prime Minister Netanyahu and I are confident that the new MOU will make a significant contribution to Israel’s security in what remains a dangerous neighborhood.” The agreement was signed at the State Department by U.S. Undersecretary of State Thomas Shannon and Jacob Nagel, who is the acting head of Netanyahu’s national security council. A White House fact sheet outlines the deal's components: -annual disbursements of $3.3 billion in foreign military financing -$500 million annually designated for Israeli missile defense, a first-time inclusion in the aid agreement. -A gradual elimination of a special arrangement that has allowed Israel to utilize 26.3 percent of the U.S. aid for its own defense industry instead of exclusively for American weapons. -The removal of a longstanding provision permitting Israel to spend about 13 percent of the U.S. aid on military fuel. -The funding will enable Israel to modernize a significant portion of its fighter aircraft, including the procurement of additional F-35 Joint Strike Fighters. Israel is set to acquire 33 F-35 aircraft, with the first two scheduled for delivery in December.

text: In eastern Syria, a deadly airstrike struck the Qusur district of Deir al-Zor city, which is controlled by the government, resulting in over a dozen fatalities, according to reports from state television and a war monitoring group on Monday. Syrian state media reported that the airstrike was conducted by jets from a U.S.-led coalition targeting Islamic State, claiming 14 civilians were killed and 32 others injured. However, a coalition spokesperson stated on Tuesday that they did not execute such an air raid, noting that their only recent operation near the city occurred in September, across the Euphrates River. The Syrian Observatory for Human Rights, based in Britain, indicated that the identity of the aircraft responsible for the attack was unclear, but at least 22 individuals lost their lives. The Syrian military, with support from Russia, Iran, and Shiite militias, is actively engaged in combat against Islamic State within Deir al-Zor and its surrounding areas. Both Syrian and Russian air forces have been targeting Islamic State in this region. Meanwhile, a coalition backed by the U.S. has been launching airstrikes against Islamic State to assist the Syrian Democratic Forces (SDF), an alliance of Kurdish and Arab fighters situated to the east of Deir al-Zor, across the Euphrates. Conflicts have arisen in recent months between the U.S.-backed coalition and the Syrian army as both sides have advanced against Islamic State, reclaiming territory in eastern Syria. To avoid potential clashes, the U.S. and Russia have indicated they maintain communication with one another.
source_text: Deadly air strike hits Syrian government-held Deir al-Zor: state TV, monitor. BEIRUT (Reuters) - An air raid in the government-held Qusur district of Deir al-Zor city in eastern Syria killed more than a dozen people, Syrian state television and a war monitor said on Monday.  State television said jets from a U.S.-led international coalition battling Islamic State carried out the air strike and that it killed 14 civilians and wounded 32 others.  A spokesman for the coalition said on Tuesday it had not carried out such a raid, and that its only strike in the vicinity in recent weeks took place in September across the Euphrates from the city. The war monitor, the Britain-based Syrian Observatory for Human Rights, reported that it was not known which aircraft carried out the strike, but that at least 22 people were killed.  The Syrian army, backed by Russia, Iran and Shi ite militias, is fighting Islamic State in the city of Deir al-Zor, as well as in parts of the surrounding countryside. Both Syrian and Russian jets have been hitting Islamic State in that area.  The U.S.-backed coalition has been conducting air strikes against Islamic State in support of the Syrian Democratic Forces (SDF) alliance of Kurdish and Arab militias to the east of Deir al-Zor across the Euphrates.  The rival U.S.-backed and Syrian army offensives against Islamic State have clashed several times over recent months as they have pushed the jihadists from territory in eastern Syria.  The U.S. and Russia have said they communicate with each other to prevent possible points of conflict of violence between the two offensives.

text: LONDON (Reuters) - A spokesperson for Prime Minister Theresa May stated on Tuesday that the UK is optimistic about swiftly reaching a framework for a transitional agreement concerning its exit from the European Union, despite ongoing significant disagreements regarding the Brexit timeline. The UK is aiming for an implementation period of approximately two years following its departure from the EU in March 2019, during which access to the EU single market would remain largely intact while new arrangements are developed. Businesses are eager to obtain the specifics of such an agreement as soon as possible to resolve uncertainties regarding the trading rules post-Brexit. The spokesperson expressed confidence in reaching an agreement on the broad outline of the implementation period quickly, though did not elaborate on a timeline for when such an agreement might be finalized. "We are clear that we want to achieve this implementation period, that we believe we can do so, and that our priority is to provide certainty for business," he mentioned. May caused some confusion among businesses on Monday by indicating that any implementation period would not be confirmed until a deal regarding Britain's future trading relationship with the EU was established, contradicting expectations that a transitional arrangement would be settled prior to any trade deal. This also underscored a notable divergence between the UK and the EU concerning the timing of a trade agreement. The UK is pursuing an ambitious trade deal with the EU to succeed its current arrangement at the conclusion of the implementation period, believing that its existing close ties with the bloc will facilitate an agreement by October 2018. However, EU chief negotiator Michel Barnier stated that negotiating a trade deal would require three years, suggesting that if talks commence in December, a deal would only be ready by the end of a transition period extending to December 2020. In response to a question regarding whether the UK still believes it could secure a trade deal by the end of next year within the two-year exit framework, May's spokesperson affirmed, "Yes." An EU official commented on the timeline proposed by the UK, indicating that the bloc aimed to define a framework for their future relationship by this time next year, allowing a withdrawal treaty to consider that future under the Article 50 legal exit process. However, the official noted that the EU would only engage in discussions about the specifics of a free trade agreement after Britain has officially exited in March 2019, due to EU regulations prohibiting negotiations on trade agreements with its own member states. The spokeswoman for May stated, "Article 50 says that the withdrawal agreement has to take into account our future relationship, so we will know the terms of our partnership with the EU by our exit," when asked about the EU official's position. "But as to the details, that’s subject to negotiation and I can’t pre-empt those."

text: SEOUL/WASHINGTON (Reuters) - South Korea stated on Tuesday that U.S. President-elect Donald Trump acknowledges the seriousness of the North Korean nuclear threat, as evidenced by his "clear warning" to the isolated nation. North Korean leader Kim Jong Un claimed on Sunday that his country, which possesses nuclear capabilities, is nearing the test of an intercontinental ballistic missile (ICBM), potentially placing some areas of the U.S. within reach. Trump refuted the assertion via Twitter, asserting, "It won’t happen." South Korea’s Foreign Ministry remarked that Trump’s statement, his first regarding the North Korean nuclear situation since the November U.S. election, could be seen as a "clear warning" to Pyongyang. Ministry spokesman Cho June-hyuck noted during a briefing, "Thanks to our proactive outreach, President-elect Trump and U.S. officials are distinctly aware of the seriousness and urgency surrounding the North Korean nuclear threat." He added, "They maintain a firm stance on the necessity of sanctions against North Korea and emphasize close collaboration between South Korea and the U.S." The U.S. State Department confirmed that North Korea continues its pursuit of nuclear and missile technologies. State Department spokesman John Kirby informed reporters, "We do not believe that at this point in time he has the capability to tip one of these (missiles) with a nuclear warhead ... but we do know that he continues to want to have those capabilities and the programs continue to march in that direction." While Trump has yet to articulate a specific policy concerning North Korea, he indicated during the election campaign a willingness to engage in dialogue with its leader, Kim. Trump’s spokeswoman Kellyanne Conway expressed on ABC’s "Good Morning America" that the president-elect was "putting North Korea on notice through this tweet and through other statements that this won’t happen." Conway stated, "He as president of the United States wants to stand between them and their missile capabilities, which experts say could be deployed to reach Seattle almost immediately." She noted that Trump had not publicly detailed how he might react to North Korea’s nuclear and missile initiatives and will not do so prior to his inauguration. "We do know that there are sanctions that are possible," Conway remarked. "They haven’t always worked. I think that China would have to have a significant role here as well." Trump has previously criticized China on this matter. On Monday, he stated that China has profited from its economic relationship with the U.S. but has failed to leverage its influence to manage North Korea. In response, Chinese Foreign Ministry spokesman Geng Shuang asserted that China has been advocating for the denuclearization of the Korean peninsula. "China’s efforts in this regard are perfectly obvious," Geng stated during a news briefing. "As a permanent member of the U.N. Security Council we have proactively participated in relevant discussions on the North Korean nuclear issue and have jointly passed several resolutions with other parties. This shows China’s responsible attitude." When questioned about Trump’s assertion that China was not aiding in curbing North Korea’s nuclear ambitions, State Department’s Kirby commented, "We would not agree with that assessment." The U.S. has historically dismissed North Korea's requests for discussions, insisting on disarmament as a prerequisite. The United States and its ally South Korea have reacted to North Korean nuclear tests and missile launches over the past year with increasingly stringent sanctions. The U.N. Security Council enacted new sanctions against North Korea following its fifth and most significant nuclear test in September. Once fully operational, a North Korean ICBM could pose a threat to the continental United States, approximately 9,000 km (5,500 miles) away. ICBMs have a minimum range of about 5,500 km (3,400 miles), but some are designed to reach further distances.

Security Council we have proactively participated in relevant discussions on the North Korean nuclear issue and have jointly passed several resolutions with other parties.  “This shows China’s responsible attitude.” Asked about Trump’s view that China was not helping to contain North Korea’s nuclear ambitions, the State Department’s Kirby said: “We would not agree with that assessment.” The United States has for years dismissed North Korean calls for talks, insisting it must disarm first. text: The case involving a Minnesota peat mine has brought property rights and environmental regulations to the forefront, as the U.S. Supreme Court seems poised to allow property owners to legally contest federal permit requirements under a national water protection statute. On Wednesday, the justices deliberated for an hour on the implications of the 1972 U.S. Clean Water Act. A majority of the eight justices appeared to lean towards Hawkes Co Inc, based in North Dakota, which is challenging an Obama administration determination that its land has wetlands. This designation necessitates permits for property owners, significantly affecting developers and landowners due to the lengthy and costly permitting process it initiates. The attorneys representing Hawkes contended that the company should have the right to dispute the necessity of obtaining a permit. Concerns about the current system's impact on property owners were voiced by both conservative and liberal justices. Chief Justice John Roberts noted that applicants ignoring a government permit finding face “great practical risk.” Liberal Justice Ruth Bader Ginsburg described the process as “very arduous and very expensive,” while Justice Stephen Breyer deemed the government’s decision regarding Hawkes’ permit as “perfectly suited for review in the courts.” Only liberal Justice Elena Kagan supported the government, expressing worries about how a ruling favoring property owners could affect other governmental bodies like the Securities and Exchange Commission. Advocates for property rights pointed out that the permitting process could last two years and incur costs up to $270,000, with penalties of as much as $37,500 daily for noncompliance. Business organizations, including the National Association of Home Builders and the U.S. Chamber of Commerce, alongside 29 states, submitted legal documents opposing the Obama administration in this matter. This case follows the justices’ unanimous decision in 2012, which allowed property owners facing Clean Water Act enforcement actions to seek court intervention prior to facing compliance or financial penalties. Last year, the Obama administration introduced a regulation detailing the extent of federal authority over water bodies, which a federal appeals court subsequently suspended after being contested by 18 states. Following Justice Antonin Scalia’s death in February, only eight justices heard this case, and a ruling is expected by the end of June.
source_text: Supreme Court sympathetic to property owner in wetlands dispute. WASHINGTON (Reuters) - The U.S. Supreme Court on Wednesday appeared likely to rule that property owners can challenge the federal government in court over the need for permits under a national water protection law in a case involving a company’s plans for a Minnesota peat mine. The court heard a one-hour argument in a case balancing property rights and environmental law, in this instance the landmark 1972 U.S. Clean Water Act. A majority of the eight justices appeared sympathetic toward North Dakota-based Hawkes Co Inc, which is fighting an Obama administration finding that its property includes wetlands. The law mandates that property owners get permits in such situations. Whether a particular plot of land falls under the law’s jurisdiction is important to developers and other property owners because such a finding triggers a lengthy and expensive permitting process. Hawkes’ lawyers argued the company should be able to contest whether it even needs to go through the permit process. Liberal and conservative justices alike expressed concern about the current arrangement’s burden on property owners. Conservative Chief Justice John Roberts said applicants who disregard a government finding that they need a permit do so at “great practical risk.” Liberal Ruth Bader Ginsburg called the process “very arduous and very expensive.” Liberal Stephen Breyer called the government decision that Hawkes needed a permit “perfectly suited for review in the courts.” Only liberal Elena Kagan expressed support for the government, raising concerns about the impact a ruling favoring property owners would have on actions by other government agencies such as the Securities and Exchange Commission. Property rights advocates said the permitting process can take two years and cost up to $270,000, with owners facing penalties of up to $37,500 a day for noncompliance. Business groups including the National Association of Home Builders and the U.S. Chamber of Commerce and 29 states filed court papers opposing the Obama administration in the case. The case follows the justices’ unanimous 2012 ruling that property owners facing enforcement action under the Clean Water Act can ask a court to intervene before being forced to comply or pay financial penalties. The Obama administration last year issued a new regulation defining the scope of federal jurisdiction over bodies of water. A federal appeals court put the rule on hold after it was challenged by 18 states. Only eight justices participated in the case following Justice Antonin Scalia’s February death. A ruling is due by the end of June.
